english: One more penalty in the shoot-out. If Gonzalo Montiel scores it, Argentina will be world champion.

In the middle of the pitch, the captain waits, huddled with his teammates. He is thirty-five. He has lost four finals with his country and, six years earlier, he had quit the national team. This World Cup final in Qatar is surely his last chance.
When Montiel runs up, the captain looks at the sky. That sky he points at after almost every goal, for his grandmother.
Twenty-five years earlier, a doctor in Rosario saw that this boy was barely growing. So every evening he injected his leg with a needle.
Almost four years after Qatar, Argentina played another World Cup final. Two days later he sat down to write a short message. In it there were two words in Spanish. Me vacié. I emptied myself.
He never talked much. He just played. So how could a quiet, too-small boy carry a whole country? It all started on a small pitch in Rosario, one day when a kids' team was one player short.
In that message he also thanked his family. Without it, no career. And the very first to believe in him was his grandmother.
It was a small neighbourhood club called Grandoli, in Rosario, Argentina. The coach, Salvador Aparicio, was looking for anyone to play.
At the side of the pitch was a woman, Celia. She came to watch her grandson Matías. She had also brought his brother, a little one of four or five.
She pointed at the little one. The coach looked at him, hesitated. The boy was tiny, much smaller than the others. But Celia didn't let go. She insisted he let him play.
Aparicio finally gave in. He put the little one on the wing, near Celia, and told her: if he cries, you take him off.
At first he barely touched the ball. But the next time, he took it with his left foot and dribbled past the boys one by one. He didn't cry. Years later he remembered scoring twice.
That day the others were two or three years older. Some were almost twice as big. It didn't matter.
Aparicio never took him off again. And from that day, Celia took him to every training and every match.

That boy was Lionel Andrés Messi. Born in Rosario on the twenty-fourth of June 1987, third son of Jorge and Celia. Yes, his mother was also called Celia, like his grandmother. His father worked in a steel factory. His mother worked in a small workshop making magnets.
He had two older brothers, Rodrigo and Matías. Later a little sister, María Sol, completed the family.
Rosario is a working city on the Paraná river, with factories, a port, and two clubs that split it in two: Newell's Old Boys and Rosario Central.

The family lived in a simple house in La Bajada, a neighbourhood in the south of the city. With his brothers he played in the street until dark. Lionel was always the smallest, and always with the ball.
He went to public school number sixty-six, near home. Years later a mural with his face appeared in the neighbourhood. It says he comes from another galaxy, and from this neighbourhood.
At home everyone called him Leo. Later, because he was so small and so fast, his family and teammates gave him a nickname. La Pulga. The Flea.
His mother said that at home he was sometimes mischievous and stubborn. He hated losing, even at cards. But on the pitch that stubbornness made him chase every ball.
His father and brothers were Newell's Old Boys fans, the red-and-black half of the city. On match days the whole family went to the stadium. Leo already knew where he wanted to play.
At six he joined Newell's Old Boys, his family's beloved club. One of his first matches ended six-nil: four goals for him.
The boys born in 1987 became a team still talked about in Rosario. It was called "La Máquina del '87", the Machine of 87. For years it almost never lost.
Sometimes before the match opponents asked for a deal: at six-nil, everything stops. Even at six-nil, Lionel was furious if he hadn't scored himself.

One of his coaches, Carlos Marconi, often tells this story. He promised Leo an alfajor, a sweet chocolate biscuit, per goal. Leo scored so much that Marconi changed the deal: two alfajores, but only for a header. Soon the smallest on the pitch scored a header. He smiled at Marconi holding up two fingers.
His teammates remember details. Before each match he cleaned his boots and taped his ankles himself, like a pro. He was eight or nine.
A teammate remembers a derby against Rosario Central. Leo kept getting past the same defender, so that defender's father shouted from the stands to bring him down.
The league counted his goals. More than two hundred in five years. In Rosario they say the real number was much higher.
His size was always a problem. Big defenders tackled him, and parents shouted to stop him by any means. He got up every time and asked for the ball again.
To spare him the knocks, his coaches told him to pass earlier. He still dribbled. If he lost the ball, he went straight back to get it.
But in 1998, when he was ten, his grandmother Celia died. The one who had brought him to football was gone.
Later he said she had been a very great love, and that he still finds it hard to talk about her. He dedicates his goals to her. Often after scoring he looks up and points at the sky.
According to his mother, after Celia's death the little boy talked to his grandmother and asked her to help him. Few people knew. He showed little of what he felt.
Without her he kept playing. He was still the best in the team. But something else was wrong, and everyone saw it. The others grew. He didn't.
Newell's sent him to see Diego Schwarzstein, a hormone doctor. The club wanted to understand why its best young player was so small.
Tests showed his body lacked growth hormone. Without treatment he would be ten to fifteen centimetres shorter than expected.
A word would follow him for many years. Small. The best player of his age in Rosario, and also the smallest.
There was a treatment: an injection in the legs, every evening without exception. It was very expensive, more than nine hundred dollars a month.
Very young, he learned to inject himself. Every evening the same ritual: a needle in the leg. A teammate saw him do it before matches, as if it were nothing.
A friend's father taught him to drive, on a country road. Lionel was only eleven.

Every month his father did his accounts. The medicine swallowed a big part of his worker's wage. Help from insurance and the club stopped. Without treatment, his son's football would end before it began.
So they looked for a club willing to pay. Lionel then went to Buenos Aires for a trial at River Plate, one of the biggest clubs in the country.
In 2026 Messi told it himself. He trained there about ten days, and River wanted to keep him. The club even offered to pay for his treatment. But Newell's first had to release him.
Never was he so close to playing for a big club in his country.
But when he went back to Newell's to ask to leave, they said no, and River's offer disappeared. It all stopped there, he says. Then help came from across the ocean.

An Argentine agent based in Barcelona received videos of a boy from Rosario. With another agent he showed them to the club, and Barcelona invited the boy for a trial. In September 2000 Lionel and his father flew to Spain. He was thirteen.
At Newell's his friends didn't know where he was. They were told: he's ill.
In Barcelona he played against bigger boys. The sporting director, Carles Rexach, came to watch.
According to one account, Rexach should have taken three or four minutes to reach the pitch. He took fifteen, unable to take his eyes off the boy.
Cesc Fàbregas was at that trial. He would later play for years with Messi. Before the match a coach told him to mark the new Argentine closely.
Cesc found him tiny. Easy, he thought. A few seconds later he was on the ground and the little Argentine was racing off with the ball.
Rexach said he told the club: sign him, without even thinking. But his bosses hesitated. The boy was foreign, very small, and needed costly treatment. Weeks passed and nobody decided anything.
For Jorge the waiting was terrible. He had left a secure job at the factory. He lived in a hotel with his son, in a foreign city, not knowing if they could stay.
After more than two months of waiting, Jorge called Rexach and was clear. If nothing was settled soon, they'd go home.
On the fourteenth of December 2000, Rexach met the agents at a tennis club in Barcelona. With no sheet of paper, he wrote a promise on a paper napkin: Barcelona would sign Lionel Messi.
A club director, Joan Gaspart, later admitted that napkin had no legal value. They had to calm a father ready to leave. And it worked.
Rexach signed it, with the two agents as witnesses. Years later it was sold at auction in London for more than seven hundred and sixty thousand pounds.
Barcelona agreed to pay for the treatment and hire his father. In February 2001 the whole family came to Spain.
At thirteen Leo didn't really understand all this. He only knew he would play, and that his injections would continue, paid for by Barcelona.
For the boy from La Bajada it was a dream. For his family it was the start of the hardest year of their life.
Nothing went as planned. As a foreigner, Lionel wasn't allowed to play official matches for months. And in his second youth match he broke his leg.
His mother, brothers and little sister were homesick. They couldn't settle, and within the year they chose to go back to Rosario.
Jorge asked his son if he wanted to go back too. Lionel said no. Later he summed it up in one sentence: I wanted to continue, and my father stayed with me.
So the family split between two continents. Lionel and his father stayed in Barcelona with part of Jorge's pay. The rest went to Rosario, for his wife and the children.
A thirteen-year-old boy now lived eleven thousand kilometres from his mother, brothers and sister.
On Sundays there was nobody. He played video games with his father in their small flat. Then, according to his biographer Guillem Balagué, he went to cry into his pillow.
My dad was always there, Messi said later, and we went through many hard moments together.
At the club he barely spoke. At his first session the coach asked his position. He whispered one word, "striker", then sat in a corner of the dressing room.
His teammates didn't know what to think. According to Fàbregas, they long thought he was mute. He wasn't. He was just very shy. He spoke little. He just played.
They called him "el enano", the dwarf. But when he had the ball, nobody laughed any more.

Slowly he found his place. His team was full of boys born in 1987 like him: Cesc Fàbregas, Gerard Piqué and others. They played with three defenders and attacked all the time. And people started calling them the Baby Dream Team.
Little by little the quiet boy began to joke. His teammates discovered someone funny, crazy about cards and video games. He hated losing at them as much as at football.
One season they almost never lost, and Messi scored more than thirty goals. Piqué, much taller, protected him on the pitch.

Their coach, Tito Vilanova, would become one of the most important men in Messi's life. One day, they say, his team led three-nil after three minutes. Tito said laughing to his assistant: what will we tell them at half-time, at eight-nil?
Every evening the injections continued. And every year he grew a little. By adolescence the treatment had done its job.
He would be about one metre seventy. Still one of the smallest on the pitch. But tall enough.
Years later his Rosario doctor, Diego Schwarzstein, put it simply: he only helped a boy grow. Messi did everything else himself.
In November 2003 Barcelona played a friendly in Porto to open a stadium. The coach, Frank Rijkaard, brought on a sixteen-year-old from the academy: Lionel Messi. On the other bench: José Mourinho.
It was only a friendly. But the boy had played for the first team. That season he went through four club teams, one after another.
His official debut came on the sixteenth of October 2004, against Espanyol. He came on late, with number thirty. He was seventeen.
At that moment he was the youngest player in Barça history in the Spanish league. Others have since broken that record. He stayed seventeen years at Barcelona.
Off the pitch he was so shy he barely spoke. An agent remembered his legs: the thinnest ever seen on a footballer.
But one man in the dressing room had already seen his talent. Ronaldinho, the best player in the world, took the quiet little one under his wing.

The other Brazilians, Deco, Sylvinho and Thiago Motta, also looked after the shy teenager. Ronaldinho sat next to him in the dressing room and invited him to the Brazilians' table. Leo says he learned a lot from them all, especially from him.
Not all were so kind. According to Frenchman Ludovic Giuly, older players tackled the boy hard in training to test him. He never complained. He got up and kept playing.
On the first of May 2005, against Albacete, Messi came on in the last minutes. Ronaldinho lobbed the defence with a pass, and Messi lobbed the keeper in turn. But the referee whistled offside.
Moments later Ronaldinho did exactly the same thing again. And Messi did exactly the same. This time the goal counted.
Ronaldinho bent down, and the boy jumped on his back. His first official goal for Barcelona. Ronaldinho said he was proud to have been there at the start of this story.

A short pause in the story. A word about me. My name is Kamil. I'm twenty-one and I've been making YouTube channels since 2014, when I was nine. Most came to nothing. A hundred thousand subscribers and the silver button, I've dreamed of it since I was little. If this story touches you, subscribing brings me one step closer to that dream. Right, back to the story.
In spring 2006, in Champions League knockout matches, Messi made Chelsea dizzy at Stamford Bridge. Two weeks later, in the return leg, he tore his thigh and left in tears.
The whole Camp Nou stood to applaud him. Rijkaard put his arm around his shoulder. Messi was eighteen.
Barcelona then won the final in Paris. Messi didn't play. He was so sad he didn't celebrate the victory. Years later he said he deeply regretted that evening.
As early as 2004 another question had arisen. Messi had lived in Spain since he was thirteen, and the Spanish federation wanted him to play for Spain.
Alerted, Argentina's youth coaches reacted fast. In June 2004 they organised an under-20 friendly against Paraguay, mainly to give Messi a game and tie him to his country.
Argentina won eight-nil. Messi said playing for Spain was really possible. But in his heart he was from Rosario.
His old academy friend Cesc Fàbregas says Leo with Spain would have been phenomenal. A few years later Spain won the World Cup without him. Argentina would wait eleven more years for a trophy.
In 2005 at the Under-20 World Cup in the Netherlands, he was the best player of the tournament. Six goals, including two penalties in the final against Nigeria. Argentina were world champions.
He also received the best player trophy and the top scorer trophy of that tournament. For the first time the boy from Rosario was champion in blue and white.
Six weeks later, in August 2005, he made his debut with Argentina's senior team in a friendly in Budapest against Hungary. He came on in the second half.

On his first ball a defender pulled his shirt. Messi freed his arm to break loose and hit the defender. The referee sent him off. He had been on less than a minute. According to the press, he left in tears.
Later he told what he had thought: I came on, I was sent off, and they'll never call me again.
That night a teammate ran to plead his case with the referee. His name was Lionel Scaloni. Remember that name: years later he will return to the story.
They did call him back. In March 2006, against Croatia, he scored his first goal for Argentina. And that summer he played his first World Cup, in Germany.
Against Serbia and Montenegro he came on and scored the sixth goal of a six-nil. At eighteen he became Argentina's youngest World Cup scorer.
That day he also set up Hernán Crespo. He already looked like he belonged.
In the quarter-final against hosts Germany, Argentina were leading. Then the coach made his last changes without him, and the match turned. Eliminated on penalties.
Messi stayed on the bench the whole match. For the first time he saw a World Cup end without him. He said nothing to the press. Once again he said little.
In April 2007, in the Copa del Rey semi-final against Getafe, Messi won the ball in his own half. He beat one player, then another, then another, then the keeper, and scored.
Starting on the right, near the halfway line, he crossed almost the whole pitch in about ten seconds, ball glued to his left foot.
In Argentina everyone recognised that goal. It was almost the same as Diego Maradona's, the country's greatest hero, against England at the 1986 World Cup. Messi was nineteen.
Barcelona won that match five-two. But in the return leg Getafe won four-nil, and Barcelona was knocked out. Even a goal like that couldn't save his team.
Those were hard years for Barça. Ronaldinho was declining, the team was losing, the club was looking for a fresh start. Messi improved every month but was often injured.

In the message written after the 2026 final there's another sentence: I swear I always gave everything. And it's true. But for a long time, with Argentina, even giving everything wasn't enough to win.
In summer 2007, at the Copa América in Venezuela, Argentina reached the final against Brazil. Messi had only just turned twenty. Brazil won three-nil.
He played the whole match without being able to do much. At the end he had to watch Brazil celebrate.
It was his first final with the senior team. Nobody could know he would lose three more before winning one.
In 2008 he wanted to play at the Beijing Olympics. Barcelona refused to release him: the Games weren't on the official football calendar. The case went to the sports court.
For Messi it was his choice: he wouldn't get another chance to play the Games. The court sided with the clubs.
But Barcelona had a new coach, Pep Guardiola, Olympic champion in Barcelona in 1992. He understood. He let Messi go.
In Beijing he scored twice, against Ivory Coast and the Netherlands.

In the final against Nigeria, before about ninety thousand people, he sent his friend Ángel Di María through with a pass, and Di María lobbed the keeper. It was the only goal of the match. Argentina were Olympic champions.

He said later that some things in football happen only once in a lifetime. These were his only Games. He ranks that gold among his most precious wins. And at Barcelona, Guardiola was going to give him a new role.
Guardiola's first decision surprised people. He told Ronaldinho, Messi's idol, that he no longer counted on him. Barça would be built around a twenty-one-year-old.
Ronaldinho left for AC Milan that summer. Before that, he told Leo to take his number ten. The quiet boy who had jumped on his back wore his number, and he was the team's star.
In May 2009 Barça played at the Bernabéu against Real Madrid. According to a book by journalist Martí Perarnau, the day before, Guardiola called Messi to his office to show him a video.
Between Real's midfielders and defenders there was a gap. Guardiola told him to start on the right, then move into that gap. And when the ball came, to charge at goal.
According to the same book, Guardiola kept this plan secret until the last moment.
Messi played neither winger nor centre-forward. He played between the two, and the defenders didn't know who should follow him. Barcelona won six-two in Madrid. Messi scored twice.
A few days later, in the semi-final at Stamford Bridge, Barcelona were losing in the ninety-third minute. Messi set up Andrés Iniesta, who scored. Barcelona were in the final.
Three weeks later in Rome, Champions League final against Manchester United. Before it, Guardiola showed them their season on video, to the music of the film Gladiator.
Before that final Leo thought of Paris, that night he had felt left out, far from the party. This time, he said, he had to enjoy it much more.
In the seventieth minute, from a Xavi cross, the smallest on the pitch jumped higher than everyone and headed it over the tall keeper Edwin van der Sar.
Van der Sar was almost two metres tall. Messi about one metre seventy. The too-small boy had beaten him in the air.
Barcelona won two-nil.
That year they won everything. The league, the cup, the Champions League, and three other trophies. Six out of six, which no team had ever done.
The sixth came in December in Abu Dhabi, against Argentina's Estudiantes. In extra time Messi scored the decisive goal with his chest.
A few weeks earlier he had won his first Ballon d'Or, the prize for the best player in the world. He was twenty-two. The too-small boy was the best.
In January 2011, in Zurich, at the Ballon d'Or ceremony, the three finalists all came from the same school: La Masia, Barça's academy. Xavi, Andrés Iniesta and Lionel Messi.
People expected Xavi or Iniesta, world champions with Spain, and Iniesta had scored the decisive goal in the final. But Messi won, for the second year running.
He said he didn't expect it, and that Xavi and Iniesta deserved it as much as him, or even more. They were the first to congratulate him.
All three spoke to the press together, and said the same thing: the prize was for the team.
Years later Xavi remembered a trip with him: a polite, humble boy, not vain at all. He would never have believed he'd become the best player in history.

In May 2011 at Wembley, Barça again beat Manchester United in the Champions League final. Messi scored with a sharp low shot from outside the box. But the most moving part came at the end. That spring defender Éric Abidal had had a liver tumour removed. Carles Puyol gave him his captain's armband so he could lift the trophy himself.

In May 2012 Guardiola coached his last home match at Barça. Messi scored all four goals. After the fourth he ran to hug him. Guardiola joked: Leo had stolen the show all season, and there was no way to be jealous.
And in December 2012 he broke a forty-year-old record. Gerd Müller had scored eighty-five goals in a calendar year. Messi scored ninety-one, including five in a single Champions League match.

Müller didn't sulk. For him Leo was a giant, and his only flaw, he said laughing, was not playing for Bayern. A few weeks later Leo sent him a Barça shirt, signed by hand: respect and admiration, hugs (lit. "I kiss you"). Leo himself said he preferred titles to records.
His life off the pitch had changed too. His partner, Antonela Roccuzzo, was a Rosario girl he had known since childhood. In November 2012 their first son was born. They called him Thiago.
Two months after Thiago's birth, Leo said becoming a father changes you completely. From now on, he said, his son came before everything.

In January 2013 he won his fourth Ballon d'Or in a row. Never seen before. But that winter Tito Vilanova was again being treated for cancer. He was his La Masia coach who had become the first team's. And Abidal had barely come back from a liver transplant. In his speech in Zurich Leo forgot to thank them. He apologised afterwards. Tito, he once said, had believed in him when he was just a kid often on the bench.
In Barcelona he was a god. With his national team it was another story.
Argentina hadn't won a major title since 1993, when Messi was six. A whole country hoped he'd end that wait.

At the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, Argentina's coach was Diego Maradona himself. In the quarter-final in Cape Town, Germany scored in the third minute and won four-nil. Messi didn't score in the whole tournament.
After the match Maradona told the press he had seen Messi crying in the dressing room.
And whoever says he doesn't love this shirt, he added, is an idiot.
Because that's what many Argentines said. He had left for Spain at thirteen. He didn't play for a club in the country. He didn't even sing the anthem before matches.
There was a name for such players: "pecho frío". A cold heart. Someone who doesn't feel enough when it counts. For many his silence proved he didn't care.
At the 2011 Copa América, at home, the crowd booed him. His father said his son was really hurt and didn't understand why he was whistled.
The coach, Sergio Batista, wanted him to play as at Barça. It didn't work. For Messi comparing Argentina to Barça was a mistake: at Barça they had played together for years.
Argentina went out in the quarter-final on penalties against Uruguay. At home the criticism continued. So he did as always. He didn't say much. He played.

In April 2014 Tito Vilanova died, aged forty-five. Six days earlier, according to his former assistant, Leo had visited him at home and they had talked for hours. The coach of his first great team was gone.

Less than two months later, at the Brazil World Cup, Messi carried his team. After his first goal, against Bosnia, he looked at the sky as he often does. Four goals in the group stage. Against Iran he gave the win in the ninety-first minute.
He was man of the match four times. Argentina were back in the World Cup final, twenty-four years later.
In the semi-final it beat the Netherlands on penalties. According to defender Javier Mascherano, without Leo Argentina would never have got there.
The final was at the Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro, again against Germany. Messi had chances, his teammates too. Nobody scored. Then in extra time Mario Götze did.
At the end Messi received the best player of the tournament trophy. Going to get it, he walked right past the World Cup itself, without a glance.
He said that trophy meant nothing to him. Later Sepp Blatter, then FIFA president, claimed Messi kept repeating to himself: the best, but not the champion.
It was his second lost final. Three years later he said it would always follow him.

In 2015 at the Copa América in Chile, Argentina again reached the final. Against Chile, nil-nil after a hundred and twenty minutes. Messi scored his penalty. Two teammates missed theirs, and Chile won.
Barely a month earlier he had won the Champions League again with Barça, in Berlin, with Neymar and Luis Suárez. With his club he won everything. With his country he always lost.
That night Chile was coached by an Argentine, Jorge Sampaoli. Two years later he would coach Argentina.
After the final Messi wrote that in football nothing hurts more than losing a final. He had lost three.
In June 2016 there was still one chance. A special Copa América held in the United States, a hundred years after the very first. The final was at MetLife Stadium near New York.
And the opponent was Chile again. Again nobody scored. Again penalties.
Messi opened the shoot-out for Argentina. Leaning back, he shot well over.
Chile won the shoot-out. It was his fourth lost final with Argentina. Three in a row, in three years.
Lucas Biglia's shot was also saved. But everyone remembered the captain's miss.
Shortly after, in the tunnel, a journalist stopped him. The quiet man said only a few words: it's over, the national team, for me it's finished.
His teammates were devastated. Sergio Agüero, his best friend in the national team, had shared his room at almost every camp for years. For him, the defeat had broken Leo.
Messi cried about twenty-five seconds on his shoulder, like a little boy, repeating: it's not for me, it's not for me.
That night, says the fitness coach, Leo was still awake at two in the morning, in tears.

Then, to his great surprise, Argentines asked him to stay. The Argentine president called him and said publicly Messi was the greatest thing Argentina had. On a rainy Saturday in Buenos Aires hundreds of people gathered at the Obelisk with banners. "Don't go, Leo."
Somewhere in Argentina, fifteen-year-old Enzo Fernández also wrote to him asking him to stay. Six years later that boy would play beside him in a World Cup final.
The country that called him cold now wanted him back. Less than two months later he announced his return. In his first match he scored.
He was asked why he was coming back. He said he loved his country and this shirt too much, and wanted to help.
Later he said why he had wanted to leave. Not only the pain of losing. Things outside football had hurt him and his family.
He admitted not knowing if he had told his father before speaking in the tunnel. At the time he just felt it had to be so.
That summer in Spain Messi and his father were convicted of tax fraud over his image rights. The prison sentence was changed to fines, as often for a first offence.
In court Messi said his father managed the money. The family had already repaid about five million euros.

In June 2017 Leo married Antonela in Rosario, their childhood city. He could have married anywhere but chose his city. About two hundred and fifty guests were there, including his Barça and Argentina teammates. Thiago and his little brother Mateo were in the front row, and his brothers and sister signed as witnesses.

On the pitch Argentina was suffering. Before the last qualifier for the 2018 World Cup it wasn't even qualified. It had to win in Quito, high in the Andes, where it had gone sixteen years without a win.

That night in Argentina the streets were almost empty. People watched in bars or at home. In La Plata the band U2 even delayed its concert so fans could watch the match on a big screen. Then in the first minute Ecuador scored, and the bars went silent.
And then Messi scored three goals. Three-one, Argentina were going to Russia. Even Ecuador's fans applauded him.
In the dressing room they sang against the critics. According to Mascherano, missing the World Cup would have been the end for many of them.
Messi said afterwards that Argentina missing the World Cup would have been madness. Now they were at peace.
Their coach Jorge Sampaoli had a famous line: Messi doesn't owe Argentina a World Cup. Football owes him one.
Russia didn't pay the debt. In the first match, against Iceland, Messi missed a penalty.
The goalkeeper who saved it, Hannes Halldórsson, was also a film-maker. He had studied Messi's penalties well before the match.
Then a three-nil defeat to Croatia. Win against Nigeria with a Messi goal: huge relief, he said.
In the round of 16 against France in Kazan, Antonela was there with Thiago and Mateo in shirts saying Papá. Argentina lost four-three. Messi again went home empty-handed.

In his 2026 farewell message he also wrote that leaving the national team had hurt him, and still hurts, in the depths of his soul. He had already known that pain, in Barcelona. There the end had begun on European nights the club wants to forget.

Everything began to break. In 2018 Barça easily beat Roma in the first leg, before losing three-nil in Rome. A year later the same script: three-nil against Liverpool at home, then a four-nil defeat there.
A few days after Anfield he defended the coach: the blame lay mainly with the players, himself included.
In 2019 he won his sixth Ballon d'Or, a record. But it didn't repair what was breaking around him.
And then in August 2020 in Lisbon, Bayern Munich beat Barcelona eight goals to two.
Ten days after Lisbon Messi wrote officially to the club: he wanted to leave. Barça refused, saying his contract didn't allow it.
His father came to Barcelona to talk to the club. Messi ended up staying one more year: he would never sue the club he loved.

About six weeks after Lisbon Barça parted ways with Luis Suárez, one of his best friends. Leo wrote that Suárez deserved a real farewell, not to be thrown out like that. But nothing surprised him any more, he added.
Then in November 2020 Diego Maradona died. Argentina mourned him for days. The man who had defended Messi after Cape Town was gone, and the country still hadn't won anything big with Messi.
That year the world was locked down because of the pandemic. In summer 2021 the Copa América was moved to Brazil at the last moment. The final was at the Maracanã, against Brazil.
Because of the pandemic the stadium was almost empty. One of the biggest matches of his life with Argentina would be played almost in silence.
The players had been away from their families for weeks. Before the final, in the dressing room, the not-very-talkative captain stood up. Someone filmed.
For years he'd been called too quiet to be a leader. That night he found his voice.

Forty-five days without seeing our families, guys, he said. He spoke of the goalkeeper, Emiliano Martínez, who had become a dad without yet holding his daughter. And to finish: let's go confident and calm, because this one we're taking home.
Martínez said afterwards he felt like crying. Another player said he was already crying and doesn't remember what came next.
In the twenty-second minute Rodrigo De Paul sent a long pass to Ángel Di María, the friend Messi had set up for Olympic gold. Di María chipped the ball over the keeper. One-nil.
For seventy minutes Brazil attacked, and Argentina held on. Messi missed the chance to make it two-nil. It didn't matter.
At the final whistle Messi fell to his knees, face in his hands. His teammates ran to jump on him, until he disappeared.
Then he called his wife and sons in Rosario. After four lost finals he finally won a title with Argentina's senior team. He was thirty-four.

After the match Di María said the curse had to end one day, and it finally had. Messi dedicated the title to his family, the Argentine people, and Maradona, who was surely cheering them on, he said, wherever he is.
A month later he was due to sign a new contract at Barça. But with its debts and La Liga rules, the club announced it couldn't keep him.
On the eighth of August 2021 he walked into a room at Camp Nou to say goodbye. Before even saying a word he started crying.
He said he wasn't ready. He and his family wanted to stay. He had arrived in that city at thirteen and was leaving at thirty-four, with three sons, Thiago, Mateo and Ciro, all born there.
Another sadness: not saying goodbye to the stadium crowd. With the pandemic he hadn't seen them for a year and a half.
He signed for Paris Saint-Germain. It never really worked. After every defeat he was booed.
One day after a defeat he went to Saudi Arabia on a promotional trip without the club's permission. Paris suspended him and he apologised on video. It was already known he wouldn't stay.

In November 2022 Argentina arrived at the Qatar World Cup unbeaten in thirty-six matches. Its coach was Lionel Scaloni, the teammate who had defended him in Budapest. Messi was thirty-five. Everyone knew: it was probably his last chance.
In the opener against Saudi Arabia he scored a penalty. Then the Saudis scored twice in five minutes. Two-one defeat. One of the biggest shocks in World Cup history.
After the match Messi came to talk to the press. No excuses, he said. The dressing room was dead. But he asked Argentines to believe in the team: we will be more united than ever.
Then, according to the players, he talked to them more than ever. The quiet captain made himself heard.
A song followed them everywhere: Muchachos, as the fans said. The players sang it on the bus and in the dressing room, with Messi.
From then on every match was a final. Against Mexico Messi opened the scoring: two-nil. Then Poland and Australia fell.
Against Australia he played his thousandth career match, and scored.
In the quarter against the Netherlands, Argentina led two-nil, but the Dutch equalised in the last seconds. Penalties, and Argentina won.
After that match the world saw an unknown Messi. In the middle of an interview a Dutchman walked past and Messi called out, with the words of Rosario's streets: "What are you looking at, idiot?"

The one called cold was on fire. In the semi-final Argentina beat Croatia three-nil. Messi scored a penalty, then dribbled past one of the best young defenders in the world and set up a goal for Julián Álvarez.
On the eighteenth of December 2022 Argentina faced France in the final. Messi scored a penalty. Di María scored the second goal.
Two-nil. Only ten minutes left. Four lost finals behind him, and the trophy was right there, very close.
And then in less than two minutes Kylian Mbappé scored twice. Two-all.
Extra time. Messi scored again. Three-two. And then Mbappé scored once more, from a penalty. Three-all.
In the last minute France had one more chance, but Emiliano Martínez stopped it with his leg. After a hundred and twenty minutes it all came down to penalties.
Messi scored his. Martínez saved one, France missed another. Then came Gonzalo Montiel's turn, for the decisive kick.
It was the moment from the start of this film. Montiel stepped up to the ball. Messi looked up at the sky. He would say he was asking God to end it.
Montiel scored. Lionel Messi fell to his knees on the grass.
He had lost four finals with Argentina. He had said stop. He had come back. And now, at thirty-five, he was world champion.
Before the trophy, the Emir of Qatar put a traditional black cloak on him. Then he lifted the cup, kissed it, and didn't let go of it.
His family came onto the pitch. His mother hugged him. His three sons ran over. He photographed Antonela with the cup.

In the final he scored his sixth and seventh goals of the tournament. Then he again received the best player trophy, the one that meant nothing to him eight years earlier after defeat. This time he also had the cup.
At this World Cup he became the first to score in the group stage, round of 16, quarter, semi-final and final.
Later on TV he said he heard the cup calling him: now you can touch me.
He said he had never rewatched the final, just highlights. At home his sons imitated goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez's celebrations.
In Buenos Aires millions of people flooded the streets. The team bus could no longer move, and the players had to leave by helicopter.

In March 2023, before leaving Europe, he had another beautiful night in Buenos Aires. For Argentina's first home match as world champions, against Panama at the Monumental, he scored his eight hundredth goal. He said he had always dreamed of this moment: celebrating with his people, at home.

That summer, at the end of his Paris contract, he made a choice that surprised everyone. Not Barcelona. Not the huge Saudi offer. A young US club, Inter Miami. Many thought he was going there to slow down.
He explained his choice simply. He wanted to step a little out of the spotlight, think more about his family. For money, he said, he'd have gone to Saudi Arabia.
First match with Miami, July 2023. Coming on in the second half, in the ninety-fourth minute at one-all, he curled a free kick into the top corner.
That night, from the bench, he smiled at Antonela and their three sons in the stands. LeBron James and Serena Williams were there too. At the goal the club's co-owner David Beckham started crying.
Soon after, Miami won the first trophy in its history. Slowing down, really? And in October he won his eighth Ballon d'Or.
In Miami he also followed his sons' football. All three joined the club's academy, and he and Antonela cheered them from the touchline, like all parents.
In 2024 Argentina played another Copa América final, against Colombia, in Miami. In the second half his ankle gave way and he had to come off.

On the bench he cried. His teammate Leandro Paredes, sitting next to him, said he couldn't even look at him, just hear him cry. Argentina won in extra time, without him. It was also his friend Di María's last match.

In September 2025 he played probably, he said, his last home World Cup qualifier, in Buenos Aires, against Venezuela. In the warm-up he struggled to hold back tears, and more than eighty thousand people chanted his name. He scored twice. Ending like that, at home, he said, was his dream.
In December 2025 Miami won the MLS Cup for the first time. On the pitch his son Mateo juggled a ball, then pointed at his father.
In March 2026 he scored the nine hundredth goal of his career. He was thirty-eight. Some said he was too old.
That night Miami didn't win and was knocked out of a continental cup. For him the result mattered more than the record. And a last World Cup was approaching.
His father Jorge had always wanted to see him play one last World Cup. But just before the tournament Jorge fell seriously ill. For the first time he wouldn't be there to watch him.
In the first match, against Algeria, he scored three times. Then two against Austria, one against Jordan. Argentina won its group easily.
After every match, the same ritual. Boots off. Phone in hand. A message from home? That way he knew how his father was.
He said nothing about it, but his father was ill, thousands of kilometres away. Later he admitted he never really felt good at the World Cup.
In the knockouts every match was a fight. Against Cape Verde, extra time.
Against Egypt Messi missed a penalty. He didn't hang his head. He set up Cristian Romero, equalised himself, and Enzo Fernández won it with a header. Against Switzerland, extra time again.
Boots off. Phone in hand. A message?
In the semi-final in Atlanta England scored first. Argentina turned the match around in the last five minutes, and in the last one Messi crossed for the winner. Two-one. Another final.
At the whistle Messi was overwhelmed. Then he went round the pitch hugging players and staff. Even his coach Scaloni was speechless.
He had scored eight goals at this World Cup. In total nobody had scored more World Cup goals, or played more matches.
The final was played on the nineteenth of July 2026 at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. The same stadium where ten years earlier he had said that for him it was over.
Before the match, in the dressing room, he told his teammates to stay calm, forget the rest and think about playing.
Spain, with nineteen-year-old Lamine Yamal and lots of young players, had the ball almost the whole match and almost all the chances.
Still nil-nil. In a video published later Messi is heard telling his team: character, everyone, character.
End of normal time: Enzo Fernández, the boy who had written him a letter, was sent off. Thirty minutes to hold on, with ten.
In the hundred and sixth minute Ferran Torres scored. Argentina couldn't respond.
Messi shot only once in the match. It was his fifth lost final with Argentina.
At the final whistle Messi sat on the grass. Yamal came to hug him. Messi told him to follow his path: the future belonged to his generation. For Yamal those words were worth as much as a gold medal.
Scaloni broke down at the press conference and had to leave. Before the final he had said Messi was the best player in football history.
And the next day Messi wrote to the fans. The pain is immense, he said, and this wound will take time to heal.
Less than three weeks after the final, in August 2026, Jorge Messi passed away in Rosario after a long illness. He was sixty-eight.
A few days later Lionel wrote him a letter, made public. It began with a simple sentence. I love you, dad.

He wrote that he had promised his father to reach the final so he would come to see it. His father couldn't come. Lionel wanted to win and bring him the trophy. But he didn't manage it. His legs had nothing left to give.
He also wrote that during the World Cup, after each match, he waited for a message from his father. When no message came, he understood it was very serious.
You were my dad, my friend, my agent, he wrote. He who had left his job in Rosario and waited for a napkin in Barcelona.
Since then, when he looks up at the sky, there are two of them up there.
On the thirty-first of August Messi published the message from the start of this film. He had written it on the twenty-first of July, two days after the final, and kept it to himself for six weeks.

In it he said goodbye to the national team. Me vacié, he wrote. I emptied myself. I have nothing more to give, and very good young players are coming who deserve their place. From now on I will be one of you.
He then added a line: today, after what happened to my dad, I am even surer of my decision.
He spoke there neither of trophies nor of finals, but of his family, the fans, and his father.

On the sixth of October 2026 he played his last match for Argentina, a friendly against Benin at the Monumental in Buenos Aires. It was River Plate's stadium. The club that once wanted that little boy from Rosario, without ever being able to have him.
About eighty-five thousand people were there. He came out holding his three sons by the hand. His mother was in the stands.
A veteran of the Falklands war sang the anthem. Messi could barely hold back tears. Tenth minute: play stopped for a long ovation, and the Benin players joined in.
He set up two goals, then scored a penalty. It was his hundred and twenty-sixth goal for Argentina, in two hundred and eight matches.
His second assist went to Nico Paz, twenty-two, one of those young players who, he said, deserved their place.
After the match hundreds of drones lit up the sky over the stadium. The boy who kept silent in a corner of the dressing room took the microphone in front of eighty-five thousand people.
First he said he was thinking of his father. Then that it was the saddest day of his career.
For weeks people had been debating the World Cup referees. Messi had stayed silent. That night he said nothing strange had happened: his team had simply given everything.
Playing for Argentina, he said, is the greatest happiness. He would like to stay there all his life. Then he told the fans he loved them and would miss them.
With his wife and three sons he went round the stadium. Eighty-five thousand voices sang: Messi don't go.
The saddest day of his career, he said. Yet in his message he had written: I leave in peace, and with pride.
He was too small. He cost too much. A foreigner in Spain, he was a stranger at home in Argentina. Later he was called too old.
Two people believed in him. A grandmother who made him play. And a father who found the money, crossed the ocean with him, and stayed.
He never played for himself alone, but for them. And when he looks up at the sky after a goal, it's them he's looking for.
That cold heart Argentina talked about was never cold. It hid its feelings. It kept everything, and showed it only in defeat, or at last in victory.
And that last final, in July 2026, hurt him more than the others. Not for one more trophy. It was what he wanted to bring back to his father.
Today he still plays in Miami. He has scored more than nine hundred goals. He no longer plays for Argentina. As he wrote, he's just one more fan.
Maybe you're the quiet one, in the corner of the dressing room. The one who, they say, doesn't care.
Leo was that boy too. He never became loud. He spoke little. He played, for those who believed in him. And when it mattered most, he found his voice. One day the whole world was listening to him.
If you're the quiet one, no need to shout. Keep playing. Your turn to speak will come.
And on the night of his farewell to Argentina, the boy who barely spoke smiled at eighty-five thousand people. I'm talking more than ever, he said, and I don't want to leave.
That summer Spain didn't only end Leo's last World Cup. Two weeks before, in Texas, it had broken the dream of another boy who wanted that trophy just as much.
A boy from a small Atlantic island, whom his teammates called the crybaby. His name is Cristiano Ronaldo, and his whole story is right here.
